1.definition: Daxing was the brand-new capital city the Sui dynasty built southeast of old Chang'an in the 580s, laid out on a strict north-south grid. The later Tang dynasty inherited it and renamed it Chang'an.
Yuwen Kai was the master architect under the Sui dynasty who designed the new capital Daxing, planning its huge grid layout, and also engineered key stretches of the Grand Canal.

2.definition: The Wordless Stele is a tall blank stone monument standing at the tomb of China's only female emperor, Wu Zetian. Famously left without any inscription, it still stands today.

The reign of Emperor Taizong (626–649), named for his "True View" reign-slogan. Tang and later historians treated it as the gold standard of Chinese governance — a model of institutional reform, military expansion, and a ruler who welcomed criticism.

"Essentials of Government from the Zhenguan Era" — a later compilation of the court dialogues between Taizong and his advisors. It became required reading for Chinese (and Korean and Japanese) rulers for centuries as a manual of model governance.

The reign-period (713–741) of Emperor Xuanzong, the absolute peak of Tang prosperity, when the equal-field system still worked, the examinations produced a steady stream of officials, and Chang'an was the most cosmopolitan city in the world.

The cultural and political high-water mark of the Tang dynasty, centered on Xuanzong's reign — the period of China's greatest poetry, court music, and Buddhist philosophy that the Chinese literary tradition celebrates above all other moments.

Daxingcheng, the planned grid-capital built by the Sui in 582 on the site that the Tang renamed Chang'an. Its rigid grid plan was copied across East Asia, most clearly in the Japanese capital of Nara.

3.definition: The grand central north-south avenue of Tang Chang'an, running from the imperial city to the southern gate. At about 150 meters (nearly 500 feet) wide, it was the spine of the capital's vast grid plan and broader than any street in any modern city.

The Sanskrit word for meditative absorption or deep contemplative focus in Indian religious practice. Transliterated into Chinese as chan, it gave its name to Chan Buddhism — and, downstream, to Zen, Seon, and Thiền.

The cultural and political high-water mark of the Tang dynasty, roughly the late 7th to mid-8th century, peaking in Emperor Xuanzong's Kaiyuan era (713–741) — the era of a million-strong cosmopolitan Chang'an and the golden age of Tang poetry, just before the An Lushan Rebellion broke the dynasty.

4.definition: Mawei Station was a post stop about 60 miles west of the Tang capital Chang'an where, during a desperate flight from rebellion, the emperor's own guards mutinied and forced the death of his favorite consort.

The Sogdian form of An Lushan's name. "An" was the Chinese rendering of his clan name and "Lushan" of his given name; in his native Sogdian he was likely called Rokhshan, meaning roughly "bright" or "luminous."

A powerful Tang frontier general of the early 8th century who governed the northeastern border region around modern Beijing. He spotted the young An Lushan's talent and made him a protégé, the patronage that launched An Lushan's military career.

The otherwise-obscure private patron who in 868 commissioned the printing of the Diamond Sutra "for universal free distribution" — making him the named sponsor of the world's oldest dated complete printed book.

6.definition: Slender Gold was a distinctive calligraphy style invented by the Song emperor Huizong, with extremely thin, sharp strokes that look like twisted gold wire. It is still practiced and admired today.

Wang Anshi's signature New Policies measure: government loans of seed grain and cash to peasant farmers at below-market rates, timed to the planting season, meant to break the grip of rural moneylenders who charged ruinous harvest-time interest.
A famous bird-and-flower handscroll painted by Emperor Huizong, depicting a parakeet on a blossoming apricot branch in his exacting court style; it now hangs in the Boston Museum of Fine Arts.

Emperor Huizong's vast artificial imperial garden in Kaifeng ("Heightened Mountain"), an extravagant landscape of piled rockeries, rare plants, and exotic animals whose construction drained the Song treasury in the dynasty's final years.

7.definition: Yue Fei's chief subordinate officer, tortured to death alongside his commander in the fabricated treason case engineered by chancellor Qin Hui in 1142.
The hill beside West Lake in Hangzhou where Yue Fei's rebuilt tomb stands, fronted by the kneeling iron statues of the officials who had him killed.
The wife of chancellor Qin Hui, cast as his accomplice in destroying Yue Fei; her kneeling iron statue stands beside Qin Hui's at the hero's tomb, where visitors have abused it for centuries.
Yue Fei's rallying cry, "give us back our rivers and mountains" — a demand to recover the Chinese homeland lost to the Jurchen, now a stock phrase for patriotic resolve.
Qin Hui's notorious answer when asked for evidence against Yue Fei: "perhaps it exists." It became the standard Chinese byword for a trumped-up charge with no proof behind it.

8.definition: A tree-lined embankment Su Shi built across Hangzhou's West Lake while serving as governor; it still bears his name and is walked by tourists nine centuries later.
Of or relating to Neo-Confucianism, the Song-era revival that built a Confucian metaphysics to rival Buddhism and became the dominant intellectual framework across East Asia for centuries.
The five most celebrated Song ceramic traditions — Ru, Guan, Ge, Ding, and Jun ware — each prized for a signature glaze or decorative effect and treated as the pinnacle of Chinese porcelain.

9.definition: Lü Wenhuan was the Song dynasty commander who held the fortress city of Xiangyang against relentless Mongol siege for six years before it finally fell, opening the way for the Mongol conquest of southern China.
The region around the eastern Mediterranean, the Levant, and the Persian Gulf — the source, in this chapter, of the counterweight-trebuchet engineers the Mongols imported to crack Xiangyang's walls.

The Latin Christian principalities planted in the eastern Mediterranean during the Crusades, where the counterweight trebuchet had been perfected — the technology that traveled across Eurasia to the siege of Xiangyang.
One of the two Muslim siege engineers (with Ismail) sent from the Ilkhanate of Persia to build the giant counterweight trebuchets that breached Xiangyang in 1273.
